content: The treatment of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) and rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (RR-TB) requires a carefully designed regimen to maximize efficacy while minimizing harm. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that patients with MDR-TB or RR-TB receive a regimen containing at least five effective tuberculosis (TB) medications during the intensive phase of treatment. This includes pyrazinamide and four core second-line TB drugs, with one drug selected from Group A, one from Group B, and at least two from Group C. If the minimum number of effective drugs cannot be achieved using these groups, additional agents from Group D2 or Group D3 may be added to reach the required total of five drugs. For patients with MDR-TB or RR-TB, the regimen can be further strengthened by including high-dose isoniazid and/or ethambutol, provided there is no high-level resistance to isoniazid. The composition and duration of longer MDR-TB regimens are determined by several factors, including the availability of effective agents, the balance of benefits versus harms, and the patient’s response to treatment. Longer regimens have been shown to improve cure rates and reduce the risk of chronic disease and mortality. The evidence supporting the effectiveness of many second-line TB drugs is primarily derived from observational studies, with limited data from randomized controlled trials. As a result, the overall quality of evidence is graded as low or very low. For adults, treatment recommendations are informed by a meta-analysis of individual patient data (IPD) from over 9,000 patients, as well as additional evidence published up to 2015. For children, recommendations are based on a pediatric IPD meta-analysis of 974 children, with data extrapolated from adults when pediatric-specific evidence is unavailable. In children with mild forms of TB, the harms associated with Group B medications (second-line injectable agents) may outweigh the benefits, and these drugs can be excluded. However, in cases of additional resistance to fluoroquinolones, Group B medications are retained. Injectable agents such as amikacin, capreomycin, or kanamycin are chosen based on their likelihood of effectiveness and implementation considerations. Streptomycin may be used as a last resort if other injectable agents are not viable, provided the strain is unlikely to be resistant. Adverse events associated with second-line injectable agents, such as hearing loss and nephrotoxicity, require careful monitoring. Hearing loss, in particular, can have a significant impact on children’s quality of life, affecting language acquisition and learning. The risk of adverse reactions increases with cumulative doses, necessitating caution in patients with prior exposure to these medications. Group A drugs, which include later-generation fluoroquinolones such as high-dose levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, and gatifloxacin, are considered the most critical components of the core MDR-TB regimen. These drugs significantly improve treatment outcomes and should always be included unless contraindicated. Ofloxacin should be phased out, and ciprofloxacin should not be used due to limited evidence of effectiveness. Fluoroquinolones generally have a good safety profile, but they carry a risk of QT prolongation, particularly when combined with other QT-prolonging drugs like bedaquiline, delamanid, or clofazimine. Group C drugs, including ethionamide (or prothionamide), cycloserine (or terizidone), linezolid, and clofazimine, are used to ensure the regimen contains at least four effective second-line TB drugs during the intensive phase. If pyrazinamide cannot be included, an additional agent from Group C or D is added. Ethionamide and prothionamide are interchangeable, as are cycloserine and terizidone. Delamanid is conditionally recommended for use in children aged 6–17 years as an add-on agent to longer MDR-TB regimens, following a WHO policy revision in 2016. However, there is insufficient data to recommend bedaquiline for patients under 18 years of age. WHO advises that all TB patients, regardless of age, with rifampicin-resistant strains be placed on an MDR-TB treatment regimen, with isoniazid included until susceptibility results are confirmed. In summary, the design of MDR-TB regimens aims to achieve high relapse-free cure rates, reduce mortality, and minimize the emergence of additional resistance while balancing the risks of adverse events.
